place_exotica.lede:
Exotica Village is the adventure and thrill-ride zone on Hon Thom within Sun World Hon Thom. It is different from Aquatopia: one is a water park, while the other is built around height, speed, movement and more intense rides.
Do not choose only by ride names. Check height limits, health requirements, current wait times and how Exotica fits with the cable car, Aquatopia and the beach in the same day.

infographic.label: SCALE
infographic.value: An adventure-ride zone inside a full Hon Thom day
infographic.note:
Exotica Village is best understood as several types of experience:
• Elevated rides.
• Motion and thrill rides.
• Observation or panoramic-view attractions.
• Queue, waiting and rest areas.
• Links to Aquatopia, the beach and the cable-car station.
Eagle Eye is promoted as a 360-degree observation attraction about 120 m high, lifting its cabin to around 80 m; published capacity is about 70 people per ride.
That scale means Exotica is not something you simply walk through in a few minutes if you want to try several attractions. Real timing depends on queues, operating status and which rides suit each person in your group.

infographic.label: HIGHLIGHTS
infographic.value: Wooden Snake Fury, Eagle Eye and seasonal attractions
infographic.note:
Wooden Snake Fury is commonly presented as one of the main thrill rides. Eagle Eye is more about elevated views than pure speed. Other rides can be added, changed or operated differently over time.
It helps to separate:
• Speed and acceleration rides.
• Height-focused rides.
• Viewpoint-style experiences.
• Attractions with stricter health or height rules.
Someone who enjoys panoramic views may not enjoy drops or high-speed spinning. Families should choose by each person's comfort level rather than pushing everyone onto the same ride type.

infographic.label: BEFORE YOU QUEUE
infographic.value: Check height, health rules and current wait
infographic.note:
Before joining a queue, check:
• Minimum or maximum height.
• Heart, blood-pressure, neck, back or pregnancy restrictions.
• Whether glasses, phones or small bags are allowed.
• Current wait time.
• Whether the ride is operating normally.
• Whether there is a convenient waiting area for anyone who does not ride.
Thrill rides can leave some people tired, dizzy or uncomfortable. Do not stack too many intense rides back-to-back just to 'get value' from the ticket.

sections.heading: Do not treat Aquatopia and Exotica as the same experience
sections.body:
Sun World positions Exotica around adventure and thrill rides, while Aquatopia is the water park. They use your energy, clothing and waiting time in different ways.
If your group spans several ages, agree on the main priority before the day begins. Anyone who does not want intense rides can spend time at the beach, a viewpoint or a rest area instead of standing around for the entire itinerary.

sections.heading: A good Hon Thom day does not require doing everything
sections.body:
The cable car, water park, thrill rides and beach all compete for the same hours. Choosing a few priorities is usually more enjoyable than running from one attraction to another.
Some workable combinations:
• Exotica + viewpoints + beach rest.
• Aquatopia + one suitable Exotica ride.
• Cable car + Eagle Eye + photos.
• One main zone, then food and downtime.

visitor_questions: Does this ride have any height or health restrictions?
Are Wooden Snake Fury and Eagle Eye operating today?
What is the current wait time?
Is there a good option for someone who does not want a thrill ride?
What time is the last cable car back to An Thoi?

place_suoi_tranh.lede:
Suoi Tranh is a nature stop close to central Phu Quoc, but the experience depends heavily on the water season. The same stream can look completely different in the wet season and during a dry spell.
The stream is commonly described as beginning in the Ham Ninh mountain range and running for about 15 km; visitors normally access only a short section inside the attraction, not the full watercourse. Some sources mention a walking route of around 1.5 km and about 30 minutes to the falls, but the actual open route should be checked on the day.

infographic.label: SCALE
infographic.value: A long natural stream, with only one section set up for visitors
infographic.note:
Think of Suoi Tranh at two different scales:
• Natural scale: the stream and feeder channels extending from the Ham Ninh mountains.
• Visitor scale: trails, bridges, stone steps, rest areas and waterfall sections that are actually accessible.
You do not need a full day. A standard visit usually means:
• Walking from the entrance or parking area into the forest route.
• Following the trail.
• Stopping at pools, rocks and waterfall areas.
• Resting or entering the water if conditions allow.
• Returning along the same general route.
A half day is usually enough, but real timing changes with walking speed, water level, trail condition and whether you stop to swim.

infographic.label: THE DECIDING FACTOR
infographic.value: Whether there is enough water
infographic.note:
Rainy periods usually make the stream fuller, the forest greener and the falls more noticeable. Some sources suggest roughly May-September or June-November as wetter-looking periods, but one fixed month range should not be treated as correct every year.
What matters more is:
• Has there been enough recent rain for the stream to be flowing well?
• Has there been too much rain, making water cloudy or access unsafe?
• Are pools and waterfall sections open to visitors?
• Is the swimming area safe and supervised?
Photos of a full waterfall capture one moment, not every month of the year.

infographic.label: WHAT TO BRING
infographic.value: Shoes with grip, light clothing and a wet-weather backup plan
infographic.note:
Forest paths, steps and wet rock can be slippery. Useful items include:
• Shoes with good grip.
• Light, quick-drying clothing.
• A waterproof pouch for your phone.
• Drinking water.
• Insect repellent if you need it.
• A change of clothes if you plan to enter the water.
Avoid smooth-soled sandals, climbing high wet rocks or standing directly under a waterfall when the flow is strong.

sections.heading: Check the season before judging the photos
sections.body:
Suoi Tranh is close enough to central Phu Quoc to fit easily into a half-day plan, but promotional images are usually taken when the forest is green, the water is flowing and the light is good.
Open Phu Quoc should not use a high-water photo as a promise of what visitors will see every day. Decide whether your goal is a forest walk, scenery, a picnic or swimming, because each needs different conditions.

sections.heading: After rain it can look better - and become more slippery
sections.body:
More water can make the stream more attractive, but it also changes rock grip and trail safety. Prolonged heavy rain can make the water muddy, increase flow or lead to sections being restricted.
The best condition is not simply 'the more rain the better'. A better window is often after moderate rain has passed, when the stream still has water but the trail is not dangerously wet.

visitor_questions: Is there much water in the stream today?
Are the trails slippery after recent rain, or are any sections restricted?
How long does it take to walk from the entrance to the main waterfall area?
Which sections are open for swimming?
Has there been any recent warning about rising water or heavy rain?
Is today's route suitable for young children or older visitors?

place_other_streams.lede:
Da Ban, Da Ngon and Suoi Tien should not be treated as three interchangeable versions of Suoi Tranh. They differ in landscape, terrain, access, walking distance and seasonal water conditions.
These are places where you should not plan from photos alone. A stream can look more impressive with more water while also becoming more slippery, difficult and dangerous. In drier periods access may be easier, but waterfalls and natural pools may be much less dramatic.

infographic.label: DA BAN
infographic.value: Broad rock slabs, easy to recognise and suitable for a light picnic
infographic.note:
Suoi Da Ban is in the Cua Duong area, around 10 km from central Duong Dong. Its name comes from the large, relatively flat rock slabs along the stream.
A visit may involve:
• The access road from the residential area toward the stream.
• Large rock slabs along the water.
• Places to sit, eat or picnic.
• Deeper and shallower water sections that change by season.
Da Ban is generally easier to imagine for families or groups wanting a lighter outdoor stop. But 'flat rock' does not mean 'not slippery'. Moss, flowing water and rain can change the surface very quickly.

infographic.label: SUOI TIEN
infographic.value: More forested, more rustic and further removed from urban areas
infographic.note:
Suoi Tien is usually described around the Ham Ninh area, with a more natural forest setting. It is not the kind of place for someone who only wants to step out of a vehicle, walk a few metres and take a photo.
The visit may involve:
• Walking on forest or dirt tracks.
• Following the stream through rocks and vegetation.
• Finding a place to rest or picnic.
• Swimming if water level and safety conditions allow.
A more rustic setting can also mean fewer services, less signage, weaker phone signal and slower access to help. Go with someone who knows the route or an operator with real local experience.

infographic.label: DA NGON
infographic.value: More waterfall sections, harder terrain and more caution required
infographic.note:
Suoi Da Ngon is often described as having several waterfall levels and more demanding natural terrain. Some sources mention around seven waterfalls, but route length and accessibility can differ by season and starting point.
This is not suitable for every traveller. Slippery ground, large rocks, climbing sections and stronger water can be difficult for anyone without terrain experience.
Do not put Da Ngon into a family itinerary just because the photos look good. Ask about the real route, walking time, difficulty and whether a local guide is involved.

sections.heading: Do not put all island streams under one label
sections.body:
Da Ban is known for broad rock slabs and a picnic-friendly feel. Suoi Tien is more forested and suits a slower nature stop. Da Ngon is more exploratory and demands more fitness and terrain awareness.
Choose by group:
• Young children or older travellers: favour easy access, shorter walking and a proper place to rest.
• Friends wanting a picnic: consider Da Ban when weather is suitable.
• Travellers who enjoy forest walks: Suoi Tien can work with good preparation.
• Experienced trekkers: only then consider harder routes such as Da Ngon.

sections.heading: More water can improve the scenery and increase the risk at the same time
sections.body:
Rainy-season conditions can make streams fuller and waterfalls more impressive. Da Ban is often promoted for roughly May-November, but that is also when paths can be damp, rocks slippery and currents stronger.
Do not treat 'more water' as automatically better. Before going, ask:
• Has there been heavy rain recently?
• Can the water level rise quickly?
• Is the access road muddy or slippery?
• Are any sections closed or inaccessible?
• Is the swimming area suitable for non-swimmers?
After heavy rain, avoid moving deep into the stream channel or standing below a waterfall. Do not camp right beside the water because levels can change quickly.

visitor_questions: Can a normal vehicle use the access road today?
How long is the walk from parking to the stream?
Are water levels and slippery rocks suitable for children or older visitors?
Has there been heavy rain or any rising-water warning recently?
Which sections are open for swimming and which should be avoided?
Is a local guide available if we go farther into the stream area?

activity_tour_3_islands.lede:
'Three-island tour' is a trip format in the An Thoi archipelago, not a fixed set of the same three islands for every operator and every day. Popular routes often mention Hon Mong Tay, Hon Gam Ghi and Hon May Rut, but the order, actual stops and time spent at each can change.
It is a full-day sea trip, usually combining speedboat or boat transfers, swimming, snorkeling, lunch and time on the islands. Quality is not about how many island names appear in the brochure. It depends on how the operator uses the day and how the route changes when sea conditions do.

infographic.label: SCALE
infographic.value: A full day at sea with several legs and stops
infographic.note:
A typical three-island tour may include:
• Hotel pickup and transfer to the port.
• Speedboat or boat travel into the An Thoi archipelago.
• One or more swimming stops.
• Snorkeling.
• Lunch and rest.
• Optional extras such as a coral park, seawalking or paid activities.
• Return to port and hotel drop-off.
From pickup to finish, the day can last around 8-10 hours. Actual time in the water is usually much shorter than total transfer, boarding, meal and rest time.
A tour advertised as 'three islands' does not mean three separate long island experiences. One stop may be mainly for snorkeling, another for lunch and another for swimming or photos.

infographic.label: QUALITY
infographic.value: Useful time in the water matters more than the number of stops
infographic.note:
A good itinerary should make clear:
• How long each stop lasts.
• How many minutes are actually available for swimming or snorkeling.
• Which stop is the main coral site.
• Whether lunch is on an island or on the boat.
• Travel time between stops.
• How many guests share the speedboat.
• Whether weak swimmers have dedicated support.
Fewer stops with enough water time can be much better than racing across several islands for 20-30 minutes each. If snorkeling is your priority, choose a tour that gives real time at the reef rather than one built mostly around photos and meals.

infographic.label: BEFORE YOU GO
infographic.value: Check the sea and confirm the boat setup
infographic.note:
Good weather on land does not automatically mean An Thoi waters are suitable. Check wind, waves, rain, underwater visibility and the operator's route-change policy.
Also confirm:
• Boat or speedboat.
• Meeting point and pickup time.
• Planned island stops for that day.
• What activities are included.
• What costs extra.
• Whether life jackets, masks, snorkels and fins are provided.
• What happens if rough sea prevents access to one of the islands.

sections.heading: Do not buy the tour only from the list of island names
sections.body:
The An Thoi archipelago gives operators several possible stops. A good tour should explain real time at sea, time at each stop, included activities and the backup plan if conditions change.
A beautiful island name does not guarantee a good visit. A beach may be quiet and clear one day, then crowded, murky or exposed to waves the next.

sections.heading: Coral is not a prop for the tour
sections.body:
When snorkeling, do not stand on coral, break it, touch it or lift marine life out of the water. Avoid feeding fish simply to gather them for photos.
Listen to instructions about where to enter the water, boat traffic and how to keep distance from the reef. A good experience is one where the ecosystem is still intact after the group leaves.

visitor_questions: Which islands are planned for today, and why those stops?
How much actual snorkeling time is included?
Which stop is the main reef site?
Where is lunch, and does the menu change by day?
What is the backup route if the sea changes?
How many guests and how many crew or guides are on the speedboat?

VisitPhuQuoc - Hòn Rỏi, lặn ngắm san hô và câu cá

activity_snorkeling_an_thoi.lede:
Snorkeling lets you observe the reef from the surface using a mask and snorkel, with fins and a life jacket depending on the tour. It is easier to access than scuba diving, but it still needs suitable sea conditions, well-fitting equipment and a guide who knows how to organise the group.
Do not reduce snorkeling to 'just put your face in the water'. Weak swimmers can panic if the mask leaks, breathing through the snorkel feels unfamiliar, the current moves them or they cannot see the bottom.

infographic.label: SCALE
infographic.value: A short activity inside a larger sea trip, not the whole tour
infographic.note:
Snorkeling is usually organised at one or more reef sites:
• Travel from the port or island to the reef.
• Safety briefing and equipment check.
• Enter the water as a group.
• Observe the reef for a limited period.
• Return to the boat or speedboat at the agreed time.
Being at the site for 45 minutes does not mean you get 45 minutes underwater. Ask how much actual water time you have, how large the group is and whether anyone stays close to weaker swimmers.

infographic.label: EQUIPMENT
infographic.value: Mask, snorkel, fins and a life jacket depending on the tour
infographic.note:
The mask needs to fit properly so it does not flood. Travellers should be shown how to hold the snorkel, breathe through it and clear water. Fins help movement but can make a beginner feel unbalanced at first.
A life jacket is not a sign that someone 'cannot swim'. It is a useful safety aid, especially with current, crowded water or anyone unfamiliar with open-sea snorkeling.

infographic.label: GOOD CONDITIONS
infographic.value: Clear enough water, manageable waves and no strong current
infographic.note:
Underwater visibility changes with:
• Recent rain.
• Wind and waves.
• Current.
• Tide.
• Boat and visitor density at the site.
• Light during the day.
A reef that looked crystal clear yesterday may not look the same today. Murky water or stronger waves can reduce the quality of the activity even if the boat reaches the planned location.

sections.heading: Easy to try does not mean risk-free
sections.body:
Someone who is not a strong swimmer can still enjoy snorkeling in the right conditions with a life jacket and good support, but nobody should be forced into the water when frightened or when the sea is poor.
Beginners should first practise breathing in calm or shallow water close to the boat before moving farther away. Young children need direct adult supervision, not only a guide watching a large group.

sections.heading: A reef changes from day to day
sections.body:
Visibility, current and boat traffic all change the experience. Do not judge a reef only from promotional photos taken on an ideal day.
When conditions are poor, shortening the session or changing location is the better decision. The goal is not to preserve the number of advertised activities at any cost.

visitor_questions: What are underwater visibility and current like today?
How much actual time will we spend in the water?
Are life jackets and close support available for weak swimmers?
Will boats or speedboats be moving close to the snorkeling area?
What happens if someone panics or wants to leave the water early?
Do I need to bring my own prescription mask or any personal equipment?

sources.label: VisitPhuQuoc - Snorkeling Hòn Thơm, 21/08/2026

activity_scuba.lede:
Scuba diving takes you below the surface with a tank and dedicated diving equipment. It is a technical activity that needs more safety procedure, professional supervision and health screening than snorkeling.
For beginners, an introductory dive may be run at limited depth and duration with direct instructor supervision. It should not be treated simply as 'snorkeling, but deeper'.

infographic.label: SCALE
infographic.value: A dive session includes briefing, equipment checks and underwater time
infographic.note:
A scuba programme usually includes several stages:
• Travel to the dive site.
• Health declaration.
• Theory briefing and underwater hand signals.
• Fitting and checking equipment.
• Diving with an instructor or guide.
• Returning to the surface, resting and monitoring how you feel.
• One or more dives depending on the programme.
Total time from departure to finish is much longer than the actual time underwater. Beginners should ask whether they are buying one introductory dive or a multi-dive programme, what depth is planned and how many guests each instructor supervises.

infographic.label: HOW IT DIFFERS FROM SNORKELING
infographic.value: You breathe from a tank underwater and deal with pressure changes
infographic.note:
Scuba lets you stay underwater longer and go deeper than snorkeling, but you need to learn how to:
• Breathe steadily through a regulator.
• Equalise ear pressure.
• Use hand signals.
• Control buoyancy and distance.
• Respond if a mask or regulator has a problem.
• Ascend under instruction.
Beginners should never descend on their own or separate from the instructor. Non-certified programmes need direct supervision, controlled depth and properly checked equipment.

infographic.label: BEFORE YOU DIVE
infographic.value: Declare health conditions and plan the time after diving
infographic.note:
Ear or sinus problems, breathing conditions, heart or blood-pressure issues, a history of fainting, recent surgery or certain medications can affect diving suitability. Do not hide health information just because you are worried about missing the activity.
After diving, do not schedule a flight or another major pressure-change activity too soon. The appropriate wait depends on the dive profile, number of dives, depth and professional guidance.

sections.heading: This is a technical activity, not simply a deeper version of snorkeling
sections.body:
The appeal of scuba is breathing underwater, seeing marine life in three dimensions and learning how to move safely below the surface.
Beginners should favour an operator that provides:
• A clear briefing.
• A proper health questionnaire.
• Well-fitting, checked equipment.
• An appropriate instructor-to-guest ratio.
• A clear procedure if someone panics or wants to end the dive early.
• Transparent information on planned depth and duration.

sections.heading: Ask about safety standards before asking about the photos
sections.body:
Find out who is supervising the dive, whether they hold appropriate training or certification, how many guests they supervise, how the equipment is checked and what happens if a guest feels uncomfortable underwater.
Do not choose only because one operator has prettier photos or a lower price. For an underwater technical activity, supervision quality matters more than the number of photo stops.

visitor_questions: What qualification does the instructor hold, and how many guests will they supervise?
Is this an introductory dive for beginners or a programme for certified divers?
Is there a health questionnaire before diving?
What depth and underwater time are planned?
How is the equipment checked and replaced when needed?
How long should I wait before flying after this dive?

sources.label: VisitPhuQuoc - Lặn biển Hòn Thơm, cập nhật 2026

activity_seawalker.lede:
Seawalking lets visitors walk underwater while breathing through an air-supplied helmet instead of carrying a scuba tank. It is designed to be easier for beginners, but it still requires instruction, controlled depth, suitable equipment and basic health screening.
'No swimming or diving skill required' does not mean it suits everyone. Water pressure, the feeling of being below the surface and the enclosed helmet can make some people anxious.

infographic.label: SCALE
infographic.value: A controlled underwater walking route with limited bottom time
infographic.note:
A typical experience may include:
• Travel to the seawalking area.
• Safety briefing and basic health check.
• Putting on the air-supplied helmet.
• Descending by steps or a platform.
• Walking a set route to observe coral and fish.
• Returning to the surface and removing the equipment.
Actual underwater time is often around 15-20 minutes in some programmes, while preparation and waiting take longer.
Ask 'how many minutes are actually underwater?' rather than only asking for the total activity duration.

infographic.label: EQUIPMENT
infographic.value: Air-supplied helmet and a controlled route
infographic.note:
Guests breathe inside a helmet often compared in shape to an astronaut helmet. It removes the need to use a snorkel or wear a tank, but participants still need to get used to pressure and to walking underwater.
The route is normally controlled and supported by staff. Do not leave the route, touch marine life or use coral as a handhold for balance.

infographic.label: ASK FIRST
infographic.value: Health, age and comfort with pressure
infographic.note:
Do not assume the activity suits everyone simply because swimming skill is not required. Ask about:
• Minimum age.
• Ear, sinus and respiratory conditions.
• Heart or blood-pressure conditions.
• Actual underwater duration.
• What happens if someone wants to come up early.
• Whether a guide stays beside participants for the whole route.
Age rules can vary between operators, so confirm directly instead of relying on one general number.

sections.heading: Designed to be accessible to beginners
sections.body:
Seawalking suits travellers who want a close look at fish and coral without learning full scuba skills. The slow walking format can also work for people who do not want to swim continuously.
Do not expect a free-roaming dive. Route, duration, depth and pace are controlled. The value is accessibility, not adventure intensity.

sections.heading: Easy to join still does not mean health can be ignored
sections.body:
Ear or sinus problems, breathing conditions, heart issues or anxiety underwater should be discussed with the operator before descending.
A non-swimmer may still participate, but they need to remain calm, listen to instructions and signal immediately if there is ear pain, breathing discomfort or panic.

visitor_questions: Who should not take part in this activity?
Is ear-pressure equalisation explained before descent?
How much actual time is spent underwater?
Does a guide stay close throughout the route?
Can a guest come up early if they panic or have ear pain?
Does the route protect coral and limit physical contact?

sources.label: VisitPhuQuoc - Những lưu ý khi tham gia tour đi bộ dưới biển

activity_big_game_fishing.lede:
Big-game fishing from An Thoi is a dedicated sea trip and is very different from a short fishing stop added to an island tour. The value lies in the fishing grounds, equipment, captain, techniques and the ability to move when current, wind or fish signs change - not in a promise that everyone will land a big fish.
This is natural fishing. Even a good crew, good boat and good tackle cannot guarantee a catch.

infographic.label: SCALE
infographic.value: A long sea trip with several hours of fishing operations
infographic.note:
A dedicated fishing trip may include:
• Transfer from the hotel to the harbour.
• Boat, bait and tackle preparation.
• Running out to the fishing grounds.
• Fishing one or more spots.
• Moving if current or fish signs are poor.
• Rest, food and handling the catch if there is one.
• Return to port.
The trip can last many hours, sometimes close to a full day. Actual rod-in-hand time may be much shorter than total duration because the boat needs to travel between fishing grounds.
Do not confuse this with an island tour that adds 30-60 minutes of casual fishing. The boat, tackle, objective and expectations are different.

infographic.label: TECHNIQUE
infographic.value: Bottom fishing, jigging or another method depending on the grounds
infographic.note:
Fishing method depends on:
• Depth.
• Current.
• Target species.
• Season and weather.
• Bait or lure.
• The captain's judgement and the angler's ability.
A trip may use bottom fishing, jigging or another approach depending on the spot. Do not assume 'big-game fishing' always means one fixed technique.
Equipment may include rods, reels, line, bait or lures, weights, hooks and fish-finding electronics. Ask about quality, quantity and condition before booking.

infographic.label: NO CATCH GUARANTEE
infographic.value: Natural fish cannot be guaranteed
infographic.note:
Wild fish depend on season, current, water temperature, bait, fishing ground and other factors that cannot be controlled. An operator can guarantee the boat, equipment, duration and support - but should not guarantee that you will definitely catch a large fish.
If there is a policy to move spots, change date or compensate in another way when fishing is poor, read the actual conditions rather than relying on verbal promises.

sections.heading: A dedicated fishing trip is not the same as a side activity on an island tour
sections.body:
A long fishing trip needs a suitable boat, proper tackle, a captain who understands the grounds and the freedom to change location when conditions are poor. If fishing is the real goal, do not choose only because an island tour includes the word 'fishing'.
Ask how much time guests actually spend fishing, whether each person has their own setup and how much hands-on help the crew provides. A serious fishing trip is more than taking guests offshore and handing out rods.

sections.heading: Sea conditions and endurance matter from the start
sections.body:
Several hours offshore can cause more fatigue and seasickness than a sightseeing trip. Participants should:
• Check wind and wave conditions.
• Eat lightly before departure.
• Prepare suitable motion-sickness medication if needed.
• Bring a hat, sun protection and drinking water.
• Ask about rest space and toilet facilities.
• Avoid excessive alcohol before or during the trip.
With older travellers or anyone prone to seasickness, consider trip duration and boat type before booking.

visitor_questions: How many hours will we actually be at sea?
What fishing tackle and fish-finding equipment are used?
Does each guest have a separate rod and reel?
Can the captain change fishing grounds based on current, wind and fish signs?
Does the price include bait, equipment, meals and any extra charges?
What is the policy if fishing is poor or sea conditions are unsuitable?
Does the boat have proper rest space, toilet facilities and life jackets?

sources.label: VisitPhuQuoc - Kinh nghiệm câu cá ở Phú Quốc

activity_squid_fishing.lede:
Night squid fishing is an after-dark sea experience: the boat leaves port, lights are used, artificial squid jigs are lowered and guests wait for squid to approach. The point is the time on the water, learning the technique and sharing the night atmosphere - not a promise that everyone will catch plenty.
The activity depends directly on sea conditions, monsoon season, tide, light, fishing area and crew experience. It should be sold as a try-it-and-enjoy-the-night experience, not as guaranteed production.

infographic.label: SCALE
infographic.value: A several-hour sea trip with more than just fishing time
infographic.note:
A night squid-fishing tour may include:
• Transfer from the hotel or meeting point to the harbour.
• Waiting to board and getting settled.
• Sunset viewing or travel to the fishing area.
• Instruction on the rod and artificial squid jig.
• Fishing after dark.
• A light meal or cooking the catch depending on the tour.
• Return to port and transfer back to accommodation.
Time on the water often lasts several hours, but the total door-to-door trip can be considerably longer. Travellers prone to seasickness should ask about time on the boat, boat type and fishing area before booking.

infographic.label: HOW IT WORKS
infographic.value: Lights, artificial jigs and a controlled lifting action
infographic.note:
Boats commonly use lights to help attract squid, then crew show guests how to lower an artificial jig, manage the line and work the lure.
Squid fishing does not feel the same as ordinary line fishing. Recognising when squid take the lure and bringing it in takes some guidance. Do not move position, cast far from the boat or handle gear while the boat is moving unless the crew says it is safe.
Depending on the tour, guests may receive their own setup or share equipment. Rod count, lure condition, standing space and crew support all affect the experience.

infographic.label: DON'T EXPECT
infographic.value: A guaranteed catch
infographic.note:
Wild squid depend on season, tide, weather, light and sea conditions. Some trips catch plenty; others catch very little or none at all.
If the tour cooks the squid caught, ask how that works: whether the catch is cooked on board, shared among guests, limited in any way and whether the meal is already included in the price.

sections.heading: A tourism experience built from the rhythm of night fishing
sections.body:
Night squid fishing gives travellers a small taste of what happens on the water after sunset: boat lights, waiting, handling a line and accepting that nature controls the result.
Some tours depart from Duong Dong, others from An Thoi, but harbour and fishing area can change with monsoon season, sea conditions and operator logistics. Do not treat the departure point written in an old itinerary as permanent.

sections.heading: Choose the harbour and fishing area according to the season and sea conditions
sections.body:
Before departure, confirm:
• Whether the boat leaves from Duong Dong, An Thoi or another harbour.
• Transfer time from your hotel.
• Whether the fishing area is in a bay, offshore or near smaller islands.
• Boat type, group size and seating or standing area.
• Wind, wave forecast and the chance of postponement.
• Toilet, life jackets and support for seasick guests.
Anyone prone to motion sickness should eat lightly, avoid alcohol and ask where the boat moves least. Children need correctly fitted life jackets and continuous adult supervision.

visitor_questions: Is tonight's departure from Duong Dong or An Thoi?
How much total time will we spend on the water?
What is the boat's maximum guest capacity?
Are sea conditions tonight suitable for someone prone to motion sickness?
Does each guest get a separate fishing setup or are rods shared?
If no squid are caught, does the meal change?
Can any squid caught be cooked on board?
Are the meal, drinking water and motion-sickness medicine included?
If weather is poor, can the tour be rescheduled or refunded?
